ledger.text: Small Research experience for eligible learners.

ledger.why: designer note: the nursing parent gets no job (no effect)

items.text: If the sea is so large, why doesn't it spill over the edge?
If a tree falls where nobody hears it, did it make a sound?
How do we know the ancestors didn't make mistakes?
Why do grown-ups say "in a minute" when they mean much longer?
If everyone learns from someone, who taught the first teacher?
Why are the oldest ruins sometimes buried beneath newer ones?
If a bird steals our berries, does that make it a thief?
Can two people remember the same day differently and both be sincere?
The teacher promises to research the answer. A child writes "ADULTS DO NOT KNOW EVERYTHING" in enormous letters.
The elder accidentally sits on the teacher's notes. Everyone spends ten minutes looking for them.
A child asks whether the teacher is allowed to give (teacher.himself/herself) homework. The class votes yes.
The lesson ends in laughter, and the teacher writes the question down to revisit when everyone has had time to think.

intro.name: The question
intro.text:
A teacher has gathered the village's children for a lesson about the island. The topic is {A}. Unfortunately, (child1) has a question that nobody expected.
The teacher {smiles confidently|looks alarmed|asks for a moment to think|pretends to search for a missing page}. Nearby, an elder who was delivering supplies overhears the discussion and offers to help.

ask.name: What to do
ask.text: The class is waiting. What should the teacher do?

choices.label: Turn the question into an investigation.
Invite the elder to share a story.
Ask the children to propose their own explanations.

q1.text: The explanation is sensible and clear. The class is satisfied.

q2.text: The teacher gives an impressive answer that is completely wrong. (Child2) notices a contradiction. The teacher apologizes.

q3.text: The teacher admits that the answer is only a guess. The children appreciate the honesty more than the explanation.

q4.text: The teacher becomes so tangled in words that the lesson ends with three more questions than it began with.

i1.text: The children make observations and discover a useful pattern.

i2.text: Their experiment fails because someone uses the measuring string as a jump rope. They try again.

i3.text: The class discovers that the answer depends on what the question means. The teacher is delighted; the children are less impressed.

i4.text: A quiet child who rarely speaks offers a careful observation. The teacher makes room for (quiet.him/her) to explain.

s1.text: The elder remembers how the same question puzzled (elder.him/her) as a child. The children are fascinated.

s2.text: The elder tells a magnificent story, then admits that it is a story, not proof. The class discusses the difference.

s3.text: The elder begins with "When I was your age..." and doesn't finish until the children are nearly old enough to be elders themselves.

s4.text: The elder and teacher disagree respectfully, demonstrating that grown-ups can learn from each other.

t1.text: The children suggest several testable explanations. The class chooses one to investigate tomorrow.

t2.text: (Child1) offers an ingenious idea, while (child2) spots a flaw. Neither takes offense.

t3.text: One child insists that all unanswered questions are caused by invisible coconuts. The teacher asks for evidence.

t4.text: The children discover they are arguing about different meanings of the same word. The teacher helps them clarify it.

g1.text: The class learns that admitting uncertainty can be the beginning of discovery.

g2.text: The elder thanks the children for making (elder.him/her) think again. The children ask whether (elder.he/she) will visit next week.

g3.text: A nursing parent listening nearby quietly smiles as (parent.his/her) older child explains the lesson to the baby.

g4.text: If the Golden Child is present, he responds through an existing supported nonverbal gesture. The class treats his contribution as meaningful without requiring speech.
